questions.stem: Why must aluminium be extracted by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon?

options.text: Aluminium is above carbon, so carbon cannot reduce its oxide
options.explanation: Only metals below carbon can be reduced by coke; aluminium sits higher, so electrolysis is the only route.

options.text: Because aluminium oxide is insoluble in water
options.explanation: Solubility in water is irrelevant; the deciding factor is the metal's position relative to carbon.
options.misconception: unrelated property used as the reason

options.text: Because aluminium is too expensive to heat
options.explanation: Cost follows from the method, not the other way round; the reactivity position forces electrolysis first.

options.text: Because carbon reacts dangerously with aluminium oxide
options.explanation: Carbon simply cannot remove oxygen from a more reactive metal's oxide; no danger is involved.

questions.stem: Which raw material supplies the carbon inside the blast furnace?

options.text: Coke, an impure form of carbon
options.explanation: Coke is charged into the furnace specifically to provide carbon for burning and reduction.

options.text: Limestone, which burns to give carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Limestone's job is neutralising acidic impurities; the carbon comes from the coke.

options.text: Hematite, the iron ore itself
options.explanation: Hematite supplies the iron(III) oxide, not the carbon needed for reduction.

options.text: The hot air blown in at the bottom
options.explanation: Hot air supplies oxygen for burning the coke but contains no carbon.
options.misconception: air mistaken for a carbon source

questions.stem: What happens in Zone 2 of the blast furnace?

options.text: Coke reduces carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide
options.explanation: At the furnace's high temperature, more coke reacts with carbon dioxide, and the carbon dioxide is reduced to carbon monoxide.

options.text: Iron(III) oxide is reduced to iron
options.explanation: That is Zone 3, where carbon monoxide does the reducing of the ore itself.

options.text: Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide
options.explanation: Thermal decomposition of limestone belongs to the removal of impurities, not to Zone 2.

options.text: Coke burns in hot air to heat the furnace
options.explanation: That is Zone 1; Zone 2 consumes the carbon dioxide made there.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of adding limestone to the blast furnace?

options.text: To remove acidic impurities from the ore as molten slag
options.explanation: Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with silicon dioxide to form calcium silicate slag that floats on the iron.

options.text: To provide extra carbon for the reduction
options.explanation: Coke, not limestone, provides carbon; limestone handles the acidic impurities.

options.text: To make the iron more pure by dissolving it
options.explanation: The limestone never touches the reduction chemistry; it deals with the sandy impurity in the ore.

options.text: To speed up the burning of the coke
options.explanation: The burn rate in Zone 1 is set by the hot air blast, not by limestone.

questions.stem: Why do modern blast furnaces run continuously rather than being started and stopped?

options.text: Because of the time and cost of getting the furnace back up to temperature
options.explanation: Restarting wastes enormous energy, so raw materials go in and products come out without interruption.

options.text: Because the reactions inside are too fast to control in batches
options.explanation: Speed is not the reason; the economics of reheating a giant furnace drive the continuous running.

options.text: Because the iron would solidify if production paused
options.explanation: Solidified iron could be remelted in principle; the decisive cost is reheating the whole furnace.

options.text: Because the slag must be removed every few minutes
options.explanation: Slag is tapped off as part of normal running; it is not why the furnace never stops.
options.misconception: by-product handling mistaken for the reason

questions.stem: Which extraction route is forced upon metals that sit above carbon in the reactivity series?
questions.modelAnswer: They must be extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds — carbon is not a strong enough reducing agent for them.

questions.stem: State the cheap reduction route used for metals below carbon, naming the reducing substance.
questions.modelAnswer: Heating with carbon: the carbon reduces the metal out of its oxide, and carbon is a cheap reducing agent.

questions.stem: Explain why the blast furnace needs no external heating once it is up and running.
questions.modelAnswer: In the first zone the coke burns in the hot air, and that burning is exothermic — it gives out heat, which keeps the furnace at its working temperature, so the reaction effectively heats itself.

questions.stem: Zinc sits just above iron in the reactivity series, and both oxides can be reduced by carbon monoxide in a furnace. Using the position-reactivity link, decide which of the two metals is harder to reduce from its oxide, and say why.
questions.modelAnswer: Zinc is the harder of the two to reduce: it sits higher in the reactivity series, so it is more readily oxidised, and reduction is the reverse of the oxidation the metal readily undergoes — its oxide holds the oxygen more strongly.

questions.stem: Why is aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite?

options.text: To lower the melting point of the mixture and save energy
options.explanation: Pure aluminium oxide melts above 2000 degrees Celsius, which would be very expensive; the cryolite mixture melts far lower without interfering with the reaction.

options.text: To make the aluminium ions more positive
options.explanation: The ion charges never change; cryolite's role is purely to lower the operating temperature.

options.text: To act as the positive electrode
options.explanation: The electrodes are graphite; cryolite is the molten solvent holding the oxide.

options.text: To remove impurities from the bauxite
options.explanation: The bauxite is purified before electrolysis; cryolite dissolves the clean oxide.

questions.stem: Which half-equation shows what happens at the cathode during aluminium extraction?

options.text: Al3+ + 3e- gives Al
options.explanation: Aluminium ions gain three electrons each at the cathode, which is reduction to the metal.

options.text: Al gives Al3+ + 3e-
options.explanation: That is oxidation of aluminium metal; extraction needs the reverse, reduction of the ion.

options.text: 2O2- gives O2 + 4e-
options.explanation: This is the anode half-equation for oxide ions, not the cathode reaction.

options.text: Al3+ + 2e- gives Al
options.explanation: The charge does not balance: a 3+ ion needs three electrons to become the neutral metal.

questions.stem: What is produced at the anode, and from which ions?

options.text: Oxygen, from oxide ions losing electrons
options.explanation: Oxide ions are oxidised at the anode, pairing up to form oxygen gas.

options.text: Aluminium, from aluminium ions gaining electrons
options.explanation: That is the cathode product; the anode handles the oxide ions.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, directly from the cryolite
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide forms when the oxygen made at the anode attacks the graphite; it does not come from the cryolite.
options.misconception: secondary reaction mistaken for the primary one

options.text: Hydrogen, from the molten mixture
options.explanation: There is no water in the cell, so no hydrogen forms; oxide ions supply the anode chemistry.

questions.stem: Why do the graphite anodes need regular replacement?

options.text: The hot carbon anodes burn away with the oxygen produced, forming carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Oxygen released at the anode reacts with the hot graphite, consuming the electrodes, so they are replaced regularly.

options.text: They dissolve in the molten cryolite
options.explanation: Cryolite does not dissolve the graphite; it is the oxygen attack that wears the anodes.

options.text: They are used up supplying aluminium ions
options.explanation: Aluminium ions come from the dissolved oxide, not from the anodes.

options.text: They melt at the operating temperature
options.explanation: Graphite survives the lowered temperature easily; chemical burning, not melting, consumes them.

questions.stem: Which single factor is named as the major expense of aluminium extraction?

options.text: The large amount of electricity the process requires
options.explanation: Electrolysis of molten compounds draws huge current, and the note names electricity as the major expense.

options.text: The price of cryolite
options.explanation: Cryolite is recycled in the cell; the named expense is the electricity.

options.text: The replacement of steel cell linings
options.explanation: The steel shell lined with graphite is long-lasting; the anodes are replaced, but the expense named is electricity.

options.text: Transporting bauxite from the mine
options.explanation: Ore transport is not the named cost; the electrolysis current dominates.

questions.stem: Starting from the ore, name the two preparation stages that ready aluminium oxide for the electrolysis cell.
questions.modelAnswer: Bauxite is first purified to aluminium oxide, and the aluminium oxide is then dissolved in molten cryolite.

questions.stem: State what happens at the cathode during aluminium extraction and where the product collects.
questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium ions gain electrons at the cathode (Al3+ + 3e- -> Al), and the molten aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell.

questions.stem: Explain why dissolving the aluminium oxide in cryolite saves the plant money.
questions.modelAnswer: Cryolite lowers the melting point of the mixture, so the electrolyte need not be heated to the very high melting point of pure aluminium oxide — the big energy cost of melting pure Al2O3 is avoided.

questions.stem: A plant engineer finds the graphite anodes must be replaced every few weeks. Explain what is consuming them, naming the two reactants involved.
questions.modelAnswer: The oxygen released at the anode (from oxide ions losing electrons) reacts with the hot graphite carbon, burning the anode away as carbon dioxide — oxygen plus carbon — so the anodes wear and need regular replacement.
